name: Abraham Lincoln
summary: A self-taught Illinois lawyer and Whig turned Republican who held that the Union is perpetual and that no state may lawfully secede, and led the Union through the Civil War. He called slavery morally wrong but at first aimed only to stop its spread, later issued the Emancipation Proclamation and pressed for the Thirteenth Amendment. He backed protective tariffs, federal support for railroads, land grants and a homestead law, and held that labor ranks above capital while capital has rights. In 1858 he rejected social and political equality of the races, and by April 1865 he favored suffrage for some Black men.

notes:
Views changed: he favored voluntary colonization of freed Black Americans in 1854 and 1862 but dropped it by 1864; he said in 1858 he did not favor Black voting or jury service, and on 11 April 1865 said he would prefer the franchise for the very intelligent and for soldiers. The later position is used where a statement touches these. Answers marked 'Inferred:' are low confidence. Racial-segregation and colonization statements were answered only where his words match the wording: his support for separation was by emigration, not segregation law inside the country, so racial-segregation-law is null.

Merged with an independent gpt-6.1-sol audit: 41 answers taken from it, 28 agreed, 0 conflicts settled by the integrator.

gpt-6.1-sol notes: Independent pass; the previous audit was consulted only for metadata, sources, notes and the authorized null list. Full active list and remaining nulls reviewed. Rhetoric is at most medium. The Hungarian resolutions are joint committee resolutions presented by Lincoln, not proof of exclusive authorship; their intervention exception is distinguished from his later practical neutrality. No position on great-power blocs, ending permanent alliances or multipolarity was found. Providence and collective repentance do not establish scriptural civil law or divine rather than popular political authority. Spiritual interpretations of the war do not establish a fundamental good-versus-evil political dualism. Gettysburg and other renewal language are insufficient for radical national rebirth after decadence. Lyceum civil religion supports a qualified sacred national community, not a religious test of national membership, ancient uninterrupted identity, or environmental stewardship. Small private farms are not cooperative common-property communities. Patent incentives and technological optimism do not establish that technology solves most human problems. Capital-created-by-labor is not a goods-value theory. Church autonomy coexists with Christian military observance; neither establishes his view of religious instruction in state schools. Gurney supports qualified conscience relief, not immunity from every general law. The 1864 platform is used because he personally endorsed it on June 27, with an express Mexico qualification. His final Black-suffrage proposal supersedes blanket exclusion in 1858; Louisiana equal schooling is narrower than comprehensive racial equality and does not retract his marriage position. His voluntary overseas colonization advocacy and pressure on Black leaders in 1862 were not a plan to deport all freed people; historians dispute when or whether he fully abandoned the policy, and the late Butler account is contested. This is not silently treated as a settled 1864 repudiation. Internal tribal removal and Grant’s departmental expulsion of Jews are not by themselves expulsion from the country of a minority seen as hostile; population-transfer remains null. The personal pledge supporting tribal removal is distinguished from formal assent alone. Modern nuclear, internet, climate and algorithmic positions remain unknown. Only rationales beginning Inferred: are historical inferences. Later pass 2026-11-13 (rules 7): sources tagged by kind. Answers that mixed acts with speeches were redone from the acts alone (Emancipation Proclamation, Homestead and Pacific Railroad Acts, Revenue Act, the Sabbath order, the Mexico treaties message, the Jewish expulsion order), the words kept as listed sources. Free-trade rested only on Wikipedia and is re-answered from his 1859 tariff letter and February 1861 Pittsburgh speech in the Complete Papers (words, so the signature of tariff acts is not cited); territorial-expansion now rests on the December 1847 spot resolutions (Volume 2). The Peoria speech is cited from the Miller Center instead of teachingamericanhistory.org. The library texts of his Papers, speeches and messages are cited or declined.
